timeline.narration: The first piece is the Payload. This carries the actual login data, such as the identity you entered — for example your email — together with the password or secret you just provided. In our map, that data can be organized as JSON or Form data.

timeline.narration: Together, these pieces answer three simple questions: what are we sending, how should it be read, and what should the system know about this attempt? timeline.narration: Now the prepared login can finally leave the phone. But before it can reach the backend, the system first needs to answer a very practical question: where should this message actually be sent?

timeline.narration: That is where DNS Resolution helps. The app usually knows a service by a readable name, but the network needs a concrete destination. Resolve turns that name into the address the request can actually travel toward.
timeline.voiceDirection: Preserve existing approved delivery and audio. This metadata is a migration placeholder: reuse authoritative existing voice alignment for any already rendered/locked shot. Speak naturally as a technical story.

timeline.narration: If that answer was already found recently, Cache can reuse it instead of looking it up again. That saves a small amount of time before the login even begins crossing the network.

timeline.narration: Once the destination is known, the request moves through Network / Transit. And this part of the journey has its own information: Network Latency tells us how much delay the trip is adding.

timeline.narration: One useful measure is RTT — round-trip time — how long it takes for information to travel out and for an answer to come back. Jitter tells us whether that delay stays consistent or keeps changing from one moment to the next.

timeline.narration: So even before the login reaches the backend, we already know two important things: where it is going, and how healthy the journey toward that destination looks.

timeline.narration: The API Gateway is the first stop for our login request after it crosses the network. It doesn't check your password. Instead, it checks whether the request can continue and where it should go next. And if something is wrong, the login can stop right here.
timeline.voiceDirection: Gentle story continuation from SHOT 04. Initial 1.25s silence before narration. 0.60s thinking pause after "going."; 0.55s after "server." Only reveal API Gateway on spoken words. Read with calm clarity; do not rush to fill silence.

timeline.narration: The request must find the right service. The app now uses version two of the login address. But the gateway still knows only version one. It answers 404. The password check never starts. Choosing where a request goes is called routing.
timeline.voiceDirection: Leave a beat after “Auth Service” so the correct path can be read. Change to diagnostic tone on the deployment mismatch; let the rejection land.

timeline.narration: The address is right, but the app sends GET instead of POST. The gateway answers 405: Method Not Allowed. POST is for sending login details. GET asks to read data. This difference is called the HTTP method.
timeline.voiceDirection: Give separate weight to POST and GET. Brief hold after “method not allowed”. Pronounce method names as words, not symbols.

timeline.narration: The app gets no answer, so it tries again and again. Soon, too many requests arrive. The gateway answers 429: Too Many Requests. A few quick requests are fine. That is a burst. A limit per minute is a quota. Together, these rules are called rate limiting.
timeline.voiceDirection: Slower for Burst and Quota, then accelerate slightly on “hundreds of automatic retries” and hold on the fact Auth Service is healthy.

timeline.narration: Some requests look unsafe. A rule stops them. But a bad rule can also stop a normal login. The gateway answers 403: Forbidden. This kind of check is done by a Web Application Firewall, or WAF.
timeline.voiceDirection: Explain WAF naturally. Pause after “legitimate login”; a clear contrast between a correct request and a false positive.

timeline.narration: The app should send a field called email. After an update, it sends userEmail instead. The gateway cannot find the field it needs, so it answers 400: Bad Request. This check is called schema validation.
timeline.voiceDirection: Give viewers time to compare email and userEmail; emphasize that this is a field-name mismatch, not incorrect credentials.

timeline.narration: Those failures were only examples. Our green request passes. Now it reaches another decision: which healthy server should receive it?
timeline.voiceDirection: Soft reassuring handoff. Pause 0.45s after "examples." and 0.65s after "passes." End on a curious question leading to Load Balancer; do not introduce the next term early.

timeline.narration: The request has now passed the API Gateway, but the system still has another choice to make. There may be several copies of the login service available, so something has to decide which one should receive this attempt.
timeline.voiceDirection: Preserve existing approved delivery and audio. This metadata is a migration placeholder: reuse authoritative existing voice alignment for any already rendered/locked shot. Speak naturally as a technical story.

timeline.narration: That job belongs to the Load Balancer. Its Traffic Distribution rules decide how incoming work is spread across the available destinations instead of sending everything to one place.
timeline.voiceDirection: Preserve existing approved delivery and audio. This metadata is a migration placeholder: reuse authoritative existing voice alignment for any already rendered/locked shot. Speak naturally as a technical story.

timeline.narration: One part of that decision is the Route Mode — the rule used to distribute traffic. For example, the system may take turns between available destinations or prefer one that currently has more room to accept work.

timeline.narration: A Hash Key can add consistency when needed. It gives the system a stable value it can use when similar requests should be directed toward the same destination instead of being placed randomly each time.

timeline.narration: But before choosing anything, the Load Balancer also needs Health Checks. A target marked Healthy is considered ready to receive traffic, while a Timeout can tell us that a target is taking too long to respond and may no longer be a safe choice.

timeline.narration: Then comes Target Choice. Instance identifies the actual running copy that can take the login, while Zone tells us which part of the infrastructure that instance belongs to.

timeline.narration: Together, Traffic Distribution answers one practical question: which healthy destination should do the work, and how do we choose it without making one place carry everything?

timeline.narration: The selected destination is the Auth Service — the part of the system responsible for deciding whether this login attempt can move toward a successful sign-in. But it cannot make that decision from the password alone.

timeline.narration: First it goes through Validation Steps. These checks help the Auth Service understand what kind of authentication information arrived, whether it can be used, and what still needs to be looked up before a decision is possible.

timeline.narration: One of those checks is Token Status. If the request carries an older proof from a previous login, the system can see whether it is Expired — meaning its allowed time has ended — or Revoked, meaning the system deliberately stopped trusting it.

timeline.narration: For a fresh login like ours, the Auth Service still needs to identify the account behind the credentials. That starts a User Lookup.

timeline.narration: The lookup needs something that identifies the account. That may be a User ID, when the system already knows an internal identifier, or a Username such as the email or account name the person entered.

timeline.narration: Together, these Validation Steps answer three questions: is there an older proof we can still trust, which account are we talking about, and what information do we still need before we can decide?

timeline.narration: That missing information lives in the User Database. The Auth Service sends its User Lookup here because this is where the system keeps the account data needed to understand who this login belongs to and whether that account can continue.

timeline.narration: The first group is User Data. Profile can contain the identity information connected to the account, while Settings can hold choices and account-specific configuration that change how that user should be treated.

timeline.narration: Together, the User Database gives the Auth Service the facts it was missing: which account this is, whether the submitted secret can be accepted, what that identity may be allowed to do, and what account state should influence the journey next.

timeline.sectionTitle: When Trust Breaks Along the Way
timeline.narration: A slow database is only one way the journey can stop. Imagine the app already has an older Expired Session from a previous login. The user may still look signed in for a moment, but once that Session timed out, the system can no longer rely on it.

timeline.sectionTitle: When Trust Breaks Along the Way
timeline.narration: If the relationship is still allowed to continue, the app may try to Refresh expired token and get a new proof without asking for the password again. But when that trust can no longer be extended, the journey falls back to Fresh Auth Required — the person has to sign in again.

timeline.sectionTitle: When Trust Breaks Along the Way
timeline.narration: Sometimes the problem is not age but the proof itself. A request may arrive with an Invalid Token because the Signature no longer checks out, the token is Malformed, or the system simply does not recognize it as something it is willing to trust.

timeline.sectionTitle: When Trust Breaks Along the Way
timeline.narration: And even perfect credentials cannot override the state of the account. If Account Status says Account Locked, perhaps after suspicious activity, the login stops there. If the account is Disabled, the system has been told not to let that identity continue at all.

timeline.narration: Think about what happens one minute later. You open another page or perform another action. The system should not ask for your password again every single time.

timeline.sectionTitle: Correct Password, But Not Logged In Yet
timeline.narration: So a successful password check has to become something the system can remember and trust after this request is gone. That is why the journey now moves toward Authentication State. A correct password proves the login attempt. It does not, by itself, keep you logged in.

timeline.narration: The Auth Service has accepted the login, but now that decision has to survive beyond this single request. That is the job of Authentication State — turning a successful check into proof the system can recognize again later.

timeline.narration: Inside Session Creation, different systems can represent that proof in different ways. One design may create a Session ID, a unique reference that points back to remembered login state. Another may issue a Token, such as a JSON Web Token — JWT — that carries enough trusted information for later requests to prove who the user is.

timeline.narration: Whichever form is used, that trust should not last forever. A TTL — Time To Live — gives it a lifetime, so the system knows when this remembered authentication should stop being accepted and the person needs to prove themselves again.

timeline.narration: Now that proof has to make its way back to the app. In a browser-based flow, it may travel inside a Cookie, and a Set-Cookie instruction in the response tells the browser to store it so it can be included automatically when the next request is made.

timeline.narration: At the same time, Response Prep gets the successful answer ready for the return journey. It may include the User Data the screen needs immediately — perhaps the user’s name or basic profile information — without sending the entire account record back.

timeline.narration: The system now has something it did not have when you first pressed Login: a trusted Authentication State that future requests can use. That changes what the app is allowed to do next.

timeline.narration: What looked like one button press has now become something much more important: the system has moved from ‘someone is claiming this identity’ to ‘this is an identity we are prepared to trust.’

timeline.narration: But being logged in once does not mean the app will keep that exact state forever. Time passes, the person closes the app, comes back later, and the system may need to rebuild enough trusted context to continue without starting the whole login journey again.

timeline.narration: That is where the Session Restore Flow comes in. Instead of immediately asking for the password again, the app can try to Use Refresh Token — a longer-lived piece of proof whose job is to help request a fresh authentication proof when the previous one is no longer usable.
